passage: Tuesday, 8 pm. Aditi's diary. Today Ishita gave me my name sign at last! It's a tiny circle by my ear, because of my earring, and everybody in the Deaf club clapped their hands in the air. Before that I always fingerspelled A-D-I-T-I, all five letters, and it made me feel slow. Ishita said the name sign is how people will call me from across the room now. I practised A-D-I-T-I with my fingers on the bus anyway. Fingerspelling is for new words, like when Sir taught us the sign for "volcano" and we didn't know the letters. I want to teach Amma my name sign tomorrow. 😊

qa.q: What is Aditi's name sign made of?
qa.a: It is a tiny circle by the ear, because of the earring.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about getting a name sign, and what else might Aditi feel about fingerspelling?
qa.a: Aditi feels happy and included, shown by the excitement and the plan to teach Amma. Fingerspelling the name also felt slow, so the sign relieves that.

qa.q: What could Aditi do next to keep learning?
qa.a: Aditi could keep practising fingerspelling for names and new words while using the name sign in the club, and ask Ishita for help with signs that are unknown.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel about giving Aditi the name sign?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels glad to welcome Aditi into the community, since Ishita explained how the sign will help people call Aditi across the room.

grounding: A young signer receives a community name sign and understands fingerspelling as a tool within a full language.

passage: On market day the little bus stop in Kalimpong was crowded, and Aparna, ten, watched her deaf friend Akash bargain for a pencil box. The shopkeeper didn't sign, so Akash pointed and wrote the price on his palm. Then he saw another friend, Prem, across the lane and made a quick shape with his right hand on his chest, his name sign. Prem grinned and signed back. When Aparna wanted to introduce her cousin "Tashi", Akash slowly fingerspelled T-A-S-H-I, then asked for a name sign idea. The others laughed and suggested a hand shape like a mountain. Akash gave Tashi a thumbs up. "That's it."

qa.q: Where was the crowded bus stop?
qa.a: It was in Kalimpong.

qa.q: What was Akash likely feeling when the others gave Tashi a name sign, and what other reading is possible?
qa.a: He probably felt friendly and included, as he gave Tashi a thumbs up. He might also have been making sure Tashi belonged since a name sign is given by the community.

qa.q: What could Aparna do to help Tashi learn the signs for Tashi's name?
qa.a: She could ask Akash and Prem to teach Tashi the mountain sign, and practise fingerspelling T-A-S-H-I together so Tashi can use both.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper see Akash's way of buying the pencil box?
qa.a: The shopkeeper may have found it different, but Akash still managed. The scene shows how communication can work through pointing and writing.

grounding: A school-age signer fingerspells a new name and uses community name signs, showing fingerspelling as part of a fuller language.

passage:
On the first day of term at the Deaf school in Bristol, a new girl stood by the classroom door, holding her bag straps tight. Chidi walked up, signed a question, and pointed at her.
She fingerspelled slowly: F-R-E-Y-A.
Chidi copied it letter by letter, grinning. Then he spelled his own name back, fast, the way he had done a hundred times.
At break the class argued about what Freya's name sign should be. Someone suggested a sign near the head, because of her springy curls. Freya laughed and shook her curls. Chidi nodded hard.
In science, Mr Owens fingerspelled a new word, V-O-L-C-A-N-O. The class had no shared sign for it yet, so everybody spelled it out until Chidi made up one with a bursting hand. Freya used it straight away.

qa.q: What new word did Mr Owens fingerspell in science?
qa.a: V-O-L-C-A-N-O, the word volcano.

qa.q: How can you tell Freya's mood changed during the day?
qa.a: She held her bag straps tight at the door, which suggests she felt nervous, but at break she laughed and shook her curls, which suggests she felt pleased and included. She may also simply have found the argument funny.

qa.q: What did the class do when a word had no shared sign yet?
qa.a: They fingerspelled it until Chidi made up a sign, which shows fingerspelling filling a gap inside a full language rather than replacing it.

qa.q: What would change for Freya if the class never gave her a name sign?
qa.a: Everyone would have to spell her name letter by letter each time, which is slower and might leave her feeling less like part of the group.

grounding: The Deaf classroom shows children fingerspelling a new name and a new word, and the community giving the newcomer a name sign.

passage:
At the school for Deaf children in Hyderabad, Class 5 had a new boy. Ramesh was asked to introduce him in front of the class.
Ramesh fingerspelled the name slowly: C-H-A-I-T-A-N-Y-A. It took a long time. A few children fidgeted and one pretended to fall asleep.
Chaitanya laughed and signed, "Too long!"
Mrs Rao asked the class to suggest a name sign. One girl touched her cheek, because Chaitanya had a deep dimple when he smiled. Another suggested something about his fast bowling.
Chaitanya picked the dimple one and practised it with a huge smile.
In science that afternoon, Mrs Rao fingerspelled P-H-O-T-O-S-Y-N-T-H-E-S-I-S. The whole class groaned. Ramesh signed, "That word needs a name sign too!"

qa.q: Why did a girl suggest touching the cheek for Chaitanya's name sign?
qa.a: Because Chaitanya had a deep dimple when he smiled.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya most likely feeling when he picked the dimple sign?
qa.a: He most likely felt happy and welcomed, since he practised it with a huge smile; he may also have felt relieved not to be spelled out letter by letter each time.

qa.q: Why is a name sign useful for Chaitanya in this class?
qa.a: It is much quicker than spelling a long name, and it shows the class has accepted him into their community.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see the long science word after the name-sign game?
qa.a: Ramesh seems amused, treating the slow spelling as a joke and hinting that the class could agree a quick sign for it too.

grounding: A school-age signer fingerspells a long name and an unfamiliar word, and the class gives the newcomer a community name sign.

passage:
At my cousin's wedding in Lucknow, I kept watching Zeenat Baji and her Deaf friends at the corner table.
When the groom walked in, Zeenat spelled something with her fingers, very quickly, and pointed at the stage. Her friends nodded, and one of them made a small sign near the chin. After that nobody spelled it again. They used that sign every time they talked about him.
I don't know sign language, so I couldn't tell what they were saying. But Zeenat's hands were fast and her eyebrows kept jumping up, like she was telling a good story.
Later she taught me to fingerspell my own name, H-A-F-S-A. She laughed when I got the S wrong, then fixed my thumb.
- Hafsa

qa.q: What did one of Zeenat's friends do after she fingerspelled?
qa.a: One of them made a small sign near the chin.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's signing suggest about her mood, and why can't Hafsa be sure?
qa.a: Her fast hands and jumping eyebrows suggest she felt excited and amused, maybe sharing a joke about the groom, but Hafsa does not know sign language and can only guess from what is visible.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try at the next family gathering?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask Zeenat to teach a few more signs, including the chin sign, instead of guessing what the group meant.

qa.q: How do Zeenat's friends seem to treat the new chin sign?
qa.a: They seem to accept it at once as their shared name for the groom, using it every time instead of spelling his name again.

grounding: An observer sees a signer fingerspell a name once before her friends settle on a name sign within their own language.

passage:
First week of term: Ojas, the new boy in the flat below, was just starting to learn sign. Ujjwal fingerspelled his own name slowly, one handshape per letter, U-J-J-W-A-L, then again faster. Ojas copied, fumbled the double J, and they both burst out laughing.
Two weeks later: At the Deaf club, Ujjwal told a whole story about his cricket match with his hands and face, quick and full of expression. Only one word, the new bowler's name, did he fingerspell. Ojas watched and saw that signing was a whole language, not just an alphabet.
Next month: The club members gave Ojas a name sign, based on the way he always pushed back his curly hair. Ojas used it proudly all evening.

qa.q: Which word did Ujjwal fingerspell in the cricket story?
qa.a: The new bowler's name.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal fingerspell his name slowly and then faster?
qa.a: Ujjwal wanted Ojas to catch it and felt patient and eager to help a beginner; laughing together over the double J shows he felt at ease.

qa.q: What could a new signer like Ojas learn from Ujjwal's story?
qa.a: That fingerspelling is for names or new words, while the story itself is told in full sign with hands and face, so learning signs matters more than letters.

qa.q: How did receiving a name sign affect Ojas?
qa.a: Ojas felt welcomed and proud, using it all evening as a mark of belonging in the club.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age signer fingerspelling a name and an unfamiliar word inside full signed storytelling, and a community giving a name sign.
